<reason>PRO built a single consistent frame — squares honor, museums remember, the plinth speaks in the city's voice — and defended it under real pressure. CON's best attack (Colston was honored for philanthropy, so PRO's "primarily" test fails) was genuinely damaging and forced PRO to shift from "what the marble was for" to "what the honor rests on," and CON exploited that slide toward Washington. But PRO's closing distinction (Colston's charity was the trade's proceeds; Washington's marble is for founding a republic) plausibly holds, and CON's own Q2 answer undercut its case: refusing to put Colston back and endorsing Bristol's horizontal, museum-displayed statue is the motion's prescribed outcome. CON's late reframe of the motion as a "blanket verdict that pre-decides every square" reads "should" as foreclosing deliberation, which is a partial strawman. PRO's frame/form answer (Klan robe in a vitrine; "the building already won") directly resolved CON's dilemma, and PRO's closing sharpened the stakes cleanly. Two clipped CON rebuttals also cost it the end of key arguments. Clear but competitive PRO win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A2 in Turn 7 answering CON's form/context dilemma: the museum's frame withdraws the civic claim before the label speaks, so the same bronze endorses less and teaches more — then PRO's closing turned CON's "the frame is whatever the city says" into a liability by insisting the frame is the plinth, sightline, and taxpayer-funded maintenance.</best_rebuttal>
